paper_title: A lightweight hybrid CNN-LSTM explainable model for ECG-based arrhythmia detection
authors: Negin Alamatsaz; Leyla Tabatabaei; Mohammadreza Yazdchi; Hamidreza Payan; Nima Alamatsaz; Fahimeh Nasimi
dataset_used: MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database; Long-Term Atrial Fibrillation (LTAF) Database (PhysioNet); combined after resampling MIT-BIH to 128 Hz
method_or_model: 11-layer 1D-CNN + LSTM (3 Conv1D/MaxPool/Dropout blocks, LSTM 32 units, dense layers, softmax over 9 classes); median-filter baseline wander removal, normalization to [-1,1], 500-sample overlapping segments, class weights for imbalance
xai_technique: SHAP (Shapley values) per class on unseen test data
train_test_split: not stated (85% train / 15% test+validation split of segmented data; patient separation not described)
key_results: Mean accuracy 98.24%; sensitivity 86.1%; specificity 97.5% over 9 rhythm classes; specificity >90% for all classes; sensitivity >80% for 6 rhythms; near-perfect AUC per class; inference 5.127 ms per rhythm on Raspberry Pi; model size 0.16 MB
findings: Lightweight CNN-LSTM classifies 8 arrhythmias plus normal rhythm with high accuracy and is small/fast enough for Holter-type devices; SHAP highlights (e.g., absent P waves, delta wave, wide QRS, discordant T wave, pacing spikes) agree with cardiologists' diagnostic criteria
limitations: Classification accuracy of some arrhythmias (poor identification/false negatives for AFIB, B and T) still needs improving; only two databases combined, more needed for reliable results; only 2-lead ECG used whereas 12-lead is clinical standard; many important arrhythmias and heart disorders not covered
scope_of_future_work: Use RR intervals and QRS intervals as additional attributes; add rule-based algorithms alongside the model; combine more databases; handle standard 12-lead ECG; extend to more arrhythmia classes
page_refs: key_results: p.1, p.4-5 (Table 3), p.5 (inference/model size), p.8; limitations: p.4 (false negatives), p.9-10; split: p.3-4

paper_title: Explainable AI (XAI) for Arrhythmia Detection from Electrocardiograms
authors: Joschka Beck; Arlene John
dataset_used: MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database; 12-lead ECG dataset by Zheng et al. (merged via SNOMED CT codes)
method_or_model: 1D CNN (3 Conv1D/MaxPool/Dropout blocks + dense layers; LSTM removed from base design for explainability); Pan-Tompkins R-peak segmentation into 0.6 s beats; classes with <2,000 samples excluded (6 classes: paced, APB, LBBB, RBBB, PVC, normal); survey of 5 clinical stakeholders on explanation format
xai_technique: SHAP explainers: Permutation SHAP, KernelSHAP, Gradient SHAP, DeepSHAP (DeepLIFT-based); saliency map vs counterfactual visualisation compared in clinician survey
train_test_split: not stated (80/20 train/validation split of beat samples; patient separation not described)
key_results: MIT-BIH: training accuracy 98.26%, validation accuracy 98.30% (macro F1 0.93, weighted F1 0.98; APB precision 0.52, F1 0.67); removing LSTM reduced performance ~1-2%; combined dataset: training accuracy 82.77%, validation accuracy 73.45% (macro F1 0.69); all 5 clinical stakeholders preferred saliency maps
findings: Clinicians preferred saliency maps over counterfactuals; Gradient and Deep explainers gave smoother, more interpretable maps than Permutation and Kernel; explanations for paced beats, LBBB and RBBB aligned with clinical understanding, but APB and PVC explanations did not consistently; static CNNs on isolated beats lack inter-beat temporal context
limitations: Model trained on individual beats lacks temporal context (APB outlier); adding 12-lead dataset dropped performance by >20%, likely due to lead/measurement differences; explanations not consistent across samples within a class; post-hoc saliency maps cannot capture higher-level temporal dependencies; XAI-medical knowledge links not validated by trained medical professionals, so suggestive only; LSTM removed because it hampers the evaluated XAI methods
scope_of_future_work: Temporal fusion architectures (especially attention-based) that integrate information across multiple time windows, are robust to irregular sampling/missing data/heterogeneous inputs, and provide intrinsic, memory-based, context-aware explanations
page_refs: key_results: p.5-6 (Tables 2-3), p.5 (stakeholders); limitations: p.8-10; split: p.4

paper_title: Automated detection of arrhythmias using a novel interpretable feature set extracted from 12-lead electrocardiogram
authors: Jibin Joy Kolliyil; Melissa C. Brindise
dataset_used: Development: 2018 CPSC training set (6,877 12-lead records; 6,400 single-label used). External test: CPSC-extra, PTB-XL and Georgia G12EC (from 2020 PhysioNet/CinC), 1,072 records
method_or_model: Handcrafted interpretable features (654 features / 60 types: rhythm, morphology, time-frequency, misc; Fourier, wavelet, cross-correlation, DTW, SVD) + XGBoost classifier, 9 classes (NORM, AF, IAVB, LBBB, RBBB, PAC, PVC, STD, STE); denoising with median filter, Butterworth filters, CWT; SHAP-based feature selection to 159 features; compared with Chen et al. CNN and Lai et al. multi-stage DL model
xai_technique: SHAP values (feature selection; global and per-class/instance-specific feature importance)
train_test_split: not stated (stratified 10-fold CV at record level on CPSC; independent external datasets for testing; patient separation not described)
key_results: 10-fold CV: weighted accuracy 82%, precision 82%, recall 82%, F1 81%; macro F1 77%; MCC 0.78; AF F1 89%, block group F1 87%, STE F1 47%. External test: weighted precision 70%, recall 69%, F1 68%; MCC 0.64; mean AUC 92% (RBBB 0.97, PVC 0.87); external macro F1 0.65 vs 0.16 (Chen CNN) and 0.63 (Lai), i.e. 48% and 2% improvement (p<0.0001 and 0.0001); 4% lower than CNN model in cross-validation
findings: Feature-based XGBoost achieves performance comparable to DL with better interpretability, training efficiency and adaptability to new data; generalizes better than benchmark DL models on external data; SHAP top features (e.g., HRV and RR volatility for AF, PR interval for IAVB, ST areas in lead 7 for RBBB) largely align with clinical criteria
limitations: Performance depends on effectiveness of extracted features; errors in denoising/morphology detection propagate; Lead 2 used as basis for morphology detection across all 12 leads; XGBoost designed for tabular data, may miss temporal dynamics; median-beat summaries lose waveform dependency information; class imbalance; reliance on accurate, consistent labels (inter-cardiologist variability); comparison constrained by lack of public implementation details; only single-label arrhythmias considered; features limited for PVC, STD, STE; ~16% lower performance on external data
scope_of_future_work: Improve denoising and morphology detection, performed independently across all leads; expand feature set (discrete cosine transform, dynamic mode decomposition); train on multiple datasets; extend features to simultaneous (multi-label) arrhythmias
page_refs: key_results: p.1, p.8-11 (Tables 3-5, Fig. 7); limitations: p.9-10, p.12-13 (Section 4.4); split: p.7-8

paper_title: An explainable deep learning framework for trustworthy arrhythmia detection from ECG signals
authors: Md. Alamin Talukder; Amira Samy Talaat; Nusrat Jahan Muna; Ammar Alazab; Mohsin Kazi; Utpal Kanti Das
dataset_used: MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database (MITDB); PTB Diagnostic ECG Database (PTBDB, resampled to 360 Hz); MIT-BIH Noise Stress Test Database (NSTDB)
method_or_model: 1D CNN (2 Conv1D layers 128/64 filters + max-pooling, dropout, dense 32, sigmoid) and DNN (dense 128/64/32) for binary normal vs arrhythmia beat classification; 1 s R-peak-centred windows; Butterworth bandpass 0.5-45 Hz, 50 Hz notch, high-pass, Z-score; class balancing compared: ADASYN, SMOTE, SMOTETomek, ROS (best: ROS+CNN, 'RCX'); optimizer and GAN-vs-ROS ablations
xai_technique: SHAP; LIME; Feature Importance Analysis (FIA)
train_test_split: not stated (evaluation on a held-out test set; split ratio and patient separation not described; balancing applied to training data)
key_results: ROS+CNN accuracy: MITDB 99.74% (precision 99.75%, TPR 99.73%, F1 99.74%, AUC 99.98%, MCC 99.48%); PTBDB 99.43% (precision 99.57%, F1 99.43%, AUC 99.98%, MCC 98.86%); NSTDB 99.98% (TPR 100%, F1 99.98%, AUC 100%); DNN on PTBDB ~96.15-96.81%; GAN+CNN on PTBDB 85.84% vs ROS+CNN 99.43%; Adam best optimizer (Adagrad CNN 80.28%); CNN training time 399.249 s on MITDB
findings: ROS consistently the most effective balancing method, especially with CNN; CNN outperforms DNN, notably on PTBDB; SHAP/LIME/FIA highlight influential time-sample features (e.g., Time_33/34/35 on PTBDB, Time_365-369 on NSTDB); authors claim new benchmark accuracy versus listed state-of-the-art works, most of which lack XAI or balancing
limitations: Framework does not incorporate feature fusion strategies or transformer-based architectures; task restricted to binary normal vs arrhythmia (all arrhythmic types merged into one class)
scope_of_future_work: Integrate feature fusion and transformer techniques for robustness and generalization; real-time deployment on edge devices for continuous monitoring; fuse multi-modal patient data (clinical records, imaging)

paper_title: Design of an Explainable Deep Learning Framework for ECG-Based Arrhythmia Prediction
authors: Deepika Tenepalli; T. M. Navamani
dataset_used: MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database (Lead II); 112,559 beat images (105,430 non-PVC, 7,129 PVC)
method_or_model: ECG-CNNTX: beats (250 samples, ~0.7 s, around R-peak) bandpass-filtered 0.5-40 Hz, median-centred normalized, plotted as 224x224 RGB waveform images; frozen ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNetB0 + single-layer 2-head Transformer self-attention block + dense sigmoid head; binary PVC vs non-PVC; Keras Tuner random search; conservative zoom/shift augmentation
xai_technique: Grad-CAM (penultimate/final EfficientNetB0 conv layer); attention weight heat maps
train_test_split: not stated (80/20 random split of beat images, 90,047 train / 22,512 test, random_state=42; patient separation not described)
key_results: ~99% test accuracy for PVC vs non-PVC; ROC AUC ~0.997; ImageNet pretraining 99% vs random initialization 95.12%; best tuning trial (Trial 3) training loss 1.0368, training accuracy 95.77%; per-metric values in Tables 3-7 not recoverable from text extraction
findings: Converting ECG beats to waveform images allows pretrained vision models; hybrid CNN-Transformer outperforms standalone EfficientNetB0 or Transformer (ablation); conservative geometric augmentation reduced overfitting; Grad-CAM heatmaps consistently highlight QRS complexes/R-peaks and atypical depolarization regions linked to PVC morphology; residual errors mostly borderline or noise-distorted low-amplitude PVC beats
limitations: Trained and evaluated only on MIT-BIH, so generalizability across populations/hardware cannot be assured; assumes reasonably clean input, not tested under heavy noise, motion artifacts or missing beats; binary PVC vs non-PVC only; real-time edge deployment needs further pruning/quantization; single-lead only
scope_of_future_work: Cross-dataset validation (PTB-XL, INCART, AFDB, hospital ECGs); multi-lead ECG; multi-class arrhythmia detection (AF, BBB, SVT); model compression (pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation) and TensorFlow Lite/ONNX deployment on wearables; denoising and uncertainty assessment; attention rollout, SHAP, LIME; add temporal context (patient history, HRV)
page_refs: key_results: p.1, p.9-12 (Tables 3-7, Figs. 4-5), p.13; limitations: p.13; future work: p.13-14; split: p.6. Page numbers are PDF pages (printed pages 200754-200767)

paper_title: An explainable deep learning framework for accurate and automated cardiac arrhythmia classification using Electrocardiogram signals
authors: P. Kavitha; L. Shakkeera
dataset_used: MIT-BIH Arrhythmia; MIT-BIH Supraventricular Arrhythmia; 12-lead ECG dataset (Konkuk University Hospital, 13,241 tests); PTB-XL; external tests on Shaoxing & Ningbo Hospital and INCART 12-lead
method_or_model: Cycle-CMCHA-GAN: cycle-consistent GAN (momentum-augmented encoder-decoder generators, dual PatchGAN-style discriminators per domain) with CNN classification head; hyperparameter optimization via hybrid Artificial Afterimage + Colour Harmony algorithm; preprocessing: 50/60 Hz notch, DWT denoising, R-peak beat segmentation, temporal features (RR, QRS, QT, ST, regularity); SMOTE + class-weighted loss; amplitude scaling/noise/time-warp augmentation
xai_technique: SHAP (feature importance of ECG features such as QRS complex, RR interval, ST segment, T-wave)
train_test_split: inter-patient (MIT-BIH DS1/DS2 protocol: DS11 train, DS12 validation, DS2 test); other datasets: train/test splits labelled 'patient-level' (Tables 11, 14, 17); 5-fold cross-validation also reported
key_results: Accuracy: MIT-BIH 99.87%, MIT-BIH Supraventricular 99.88%, 12-lead 99.88%, PTB-XL 99.88%; external Shaoxing & Ningbo 98.78%, INCART 98.67%; 5-fold CV accuracy 99.58 +/- 0.08%; MIT-BIH class-wise F1: Normal 98.8, Ventricular 88.3, Supraventricular 91.9, Fusion 83.8, Unknown 77.6; 5.0 M params, 2.1 GFLOPs, 99.93% accuracy (Table 20); paired t-test vs CNN-LSTM p<0.0001; ablation: without denoising 95%, without momentum generator 97%; Table 19 mean accuracy 97%, specificity 98.7%, entropy 0.71
findings: Proposed GAN-based framework reported to outperform compared methods (ACoBi-LSTM, AlexNet, CNN-BiLSTM, BiLSTM, FFT+CNN+LSTM, MVKT, SRB-GCAB, etc.) on all four datasets; SHAP identifies QRS complex (0.350) and RR interval (0.290) as top MIT-BIH features, ST-segment (0.360) top for PTB-XL, P-wave morphology (0.330) top for supraventricular dataset; every module contributes in ablation
limitations: Lack of clinical and multicenter validation, limiting assessment of robustness across patient populations and acquisition conditions; real-world applicability not validated; more experimental testing needed. [Reviewer note, not stated by authors: overall accuracy (99.87%) is hard to reconcile with reported class-wise F1 of 77.6-88.3% for minority classes and Table 19 mean accuracy of 97%; Data availability statement says 'No data was used']
scope_of_future_work: Secure federated learning across institutions; edge-based deployment for wearables/IoT real-time monitoring; integration of multimodal physiological signals (PPG, heart sounds, respiration) for rare/complex arrhythmias and patient-specific classification

paper_title: A review on deep learning methods for ECG arrhythmia classification
authors: Zahra Ebrahimi; Mohammad Loni; Masoud Daneshtalab; Arash Gharehbaghi
dataset_used: Review (no own experiments); catalogues databases used by reviewed studies: PhysioNet/CinC Challenge, MIT-BIH Arrhythmia (MITDB), PTB, SVDB, ECG-ID, MIT-BIH AF, CUDB, VFDB, UCI arrhythmia, LTSTDB, INCART, Fantasia, MIT-BIH NSR, etc.
method_or_model: Topical literature survey of DL-based ECG arrhythmia classification published 2017-2018 (PubMed and Google Scholar; keywords DL/DNN/CNN/DBN/RNN/LSTM/GRU + ECG); 77 publications found, 2 excluded (noise removal), 75 analysed (5 surveys); categorized by DL model (MLP, CNN, DBN, RNN, LSTM, GRU), by role (feature extraction / classification / both) and by arrhythmia
xai_technique: not stated
train_test_split: not stated (review; individual reviewed studies mention patient-specific paradigms, e.g., Liu et al. 2018, Zhang et al. 2017)
key_results: CNN used for feature extraction in 52% of studies; AF and SVEB/VEB the most considered arrhythmias (48% and 21%); best reported accuracies: AF 100% (GRU/LSTM, Sujadevi et al.), SVEB 99.8% (CNN), VEB 99.7% (LSTM); e.g., Sannino & De Pietro MLP 99.09% test accuracy; Liu et al. MFB-CNN MI detection 99.95% class-based vs 98.79% patient-specific; Faust et al. LSTM AF 98.51% (10-fold CV) and 99.77% (blindfold)
findings: CNN is the dominant and most effective DL method; dynamic classifiers able to learn both short- and long-term signal content (e.g., LSTM) suit beat-level and rhythm-level variations; DL as a feature extractor alone did not give excellent results for abnormal-beat detection; computational complexity summarized (CNN high, MLP/RNN/LSTM medium, DBN/GRU low)
limitations: Limitations of DL methods identified: overfitting on small datasets; tendency to learn noise/peculiarities of ECG; computationally intensive with large memory footprint, hard to deploy on low-power wearables; vanishing gradients in deep models; effective only for a limited number of classes (~6); patient physical state (age, gender, lifestyle) excluded. Review scope limited to studies from 2017-2018
scope_of_future_work: Dynamic classification methods able to learn short- and long-term signal content efficiently; CNN-based methods expected to remain among the most efficient tools; deep time-growing neural networks not yet studied for ECG
page_refs: key_results: p.1 (abstract), p.8-9 (Section 8), p.9-10 (Section 9.2, Fig. 10); limitations: p.10 (Section 9.5); methodology: p.7

paper_title: Deep learning for ECG Arrhythmia detection and classification: an overview of progress for period 2017-2023
authors: Yaqoob Ansari; Omar Mourad; Khalid Qaraqe; Erchin Serpedin
dataset_used: Review (no own experiments); summarizes 17 databases: CUDB, NSTDB, INCARTDB, LTAFDB, MIT-BIH Arrhythmia, MIT-BIH AF, MIT-BIH NSR, MIT-BIH Malignant Ventricular Ectopy, SVDB, SCDDB, NSRDB, Georgia 12-lead, Apnea-ECG, PTB Diagnostic, European ST-T, PhysioNet/CinC 2017, CPSC 2018
method_or_model: Systematic review (Jan 2017-Jan 2023) of Google Scholar, PubMed, Scopus, DBLP; 4,215 studies identified, 2,492 unique, 78 included; inclusion required DL for arrhythmia classification with ECG and accuracy >= 96%; screened by two reviewers, validated by a third; reviews MLP, CNN, RNN, LSTM, GRU, DBN and Transformer models; proposes a 6-stage guideline pipeline
xai_technique: not stated (paper notes interpretability is overlooked and recommends interpretable DL models)
train_test_split: not stated (review; guideline recommends k-fold cross-validation and INCART for generalization assessment)
key_results: 78 papers included; Table 3: reviewed models' accuracies range 96.00-99.80% (e.g., Wang et al. 2019 GRNN 99.80% Acc, 99.40% Se, 99.90% Sp; Sannino & De Pietro 2018 DNN 99.68%); Table 4: F1-scores 95.30-99.99% (e.g., Sujadevi et al. GRU 99.99%, Xiang et al. 1D CNN 99.99%)
findings: CNNs traditionally top DL models for ECG; hybrid models (CNN feature extractor followed by RNN/Transformer) perform better than shallow DL but increase computational complexity; transformers show promising early results; limitations of database size/diversity outweigh choice of algorithm; class imbalance with over-represented normal class is a major long-term challenge; MIT-BIH remains comparison baseline
limitations: Review protocol not registered; formal risk of bias assessment not conducted; only studies with >=96% performance included (deliberately focuses on high-performing works); non-English and non-full-text studies excluded. Limitations of reviewed works: need for individually annotated beats, class imbalance, long feature extraction time, under-represented beat types, limited rich databases, training time cost, dependence on peak detection accuracy, small datasets
scope_of_future_work: Interpretable DL models; integration with active and reinforcement learning; systematic architecture/hyperparameter optimization; strategies for many-class problems (attention, focal loss); personalized detection; balanced comprehensive datasets; denoising and augmentation; multimodal data fusion and real-time self-adapting models; ViT and MLP-Mixer hybrids; standardized evaluation pipeline (MIT-BIH standard metrics, INCART generalization, R-peak jitter robustness, k-fold CV)

dataset_used: Review (no own experiments); analyses databases used by reviewed studies: MITDB (223 studies), AFDB (26), PTB (24), PTB-XL (15), NSRDB (15), INCART (11), BIDMC, VFDB, Chapman, Fantasia, UCI, NSTDB, CUDB, AHA, CCDD, QT, European ST-T

xai_technique: not stated (review notes interpretability is generally not discussed in reviewed works)

paper_title: A Systematic Review of ECG Arrhythmia Classification: Adherence to Standards, Fair Evaluation, and Embedded Feasibility
authors: Guilherme A. L. Silva; Pedro H. L. Silva; Gladston J. P. Moreira; Vander L. S. Freitas; Jadson C. Gertrudes; Eduardo J. S. Luz

method_or_model: Systematic review of Web of Science (query 'ECG classification' OR 'arrhythmia detection', 2017-2024, impact factor >1, SCI-EXPANDED); 1,427 -> 927 -> 653 -> 621 papers; 122 included (100 most-cited incl. top-10 per 2022/2023/2024, plus 22 embedded-feasibility studies); assesses E3C criteria (AAMI compliance, inter-patient paradigm, MIT-BIH, embedded feasibility); reviews pruning, quantization, lightweight architectures, FPGA acceleration, on-device learning; citation network analysis

train_test_split: inter-patient (review evaluates adherence to De Chazal inter-patient paradigm; 37/122 reviewed studies adhered)

paper_title: Recent advances in deep learning based arrhythmia classification using ECG and PPG signals: a systematic review

paper_title: Dual-branch bidirectional attention fusion of temporal and hierarchical representations for robust ECG arrhythmia classification
authors: Basheer A. Hassoon; Shengwu Xiong; Mushtaq A. Hasson; Ridwan Salahudeen; Aminu Onimisi Abdulsalami; Tauqeer Khan
dataset_used: MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database (MLII, AAMI N/S/V/F/Q); transfer targets: PTB Diagnostic (Lead II, normal/abnormal), INCART (Lead II), MIT-BIH Supraventricular (SVDB, ECG1); all resampled to 360 Hz
method_or_model: Dual-branch model: low-level multi-scale CNN (kernels 3/5/7) + squeeze-and-excitation + 2-layer BiLSTM with residual; high-level Capsule Network (primary/secondary/class capsules, dynamic routing R=5) with multi-head self-attention over class capsules; Adaptive Multi-head Bi-Directional Attention Fusion (AMBAF) with feature-wise gating; Enhanced Adaptive Margin Context Loss (EAMCL) with class-frequency-dependent margins (no oversampling); beat segmentation via R-peak thresholding, 0-1 normalization
xai_technique: Post-hoc branch contribution weights at the fusion stage (normalized mean absolute activations of each branch)
train_test_split: inter-patient (80% of subjects train/development, 20% of subjects test, no beats from the same patient in both; 20% of training portion as validation; 10-fold patient-level CV within training portion for stability only)
key_results: MIT-BIH test: accuracy, precision, recall and F1 99.55 +/- 0.06%; per-class F1: N 99.81%, S 95.37%, V 98.62%, F 90.06%, Q 99.84%; ablation: BiLSTM only 98.62%, Capsule only 98.49%, static-mean fusion 65.27%, concatenation 98.18%, bidirectional fusion 99.55%; transfer (fine-tune): INCART 99.33%, SVDB 98.04%, PTB 98.86% (linear probe 93.74%, 89.23%, 90.10%); EAMCL >2% F1 over baseline losses; 3.78 M params, 15.61 MB, 50.74 MFLOPs; AWGN: F1 32.46% at 5 dB, 25.46% at 0 dB; 95% Wilson CI fused accuracy [99.54, 99.70] on N=21,891 test beats; branch contributions 0.710 (BiLSTM) vs 0.290 (CapsNet)

scope_of_future_work: Noise-aware training (multi-SNR augmentation, curriculum noise); signal-quality-guided fusion; front-end denoising or robustness regularization; broader validation on additional datasets and acquisition settings; efficiency improvements (pruning, quantization, architecture refinement) for resource-constrained deployment

paper_title: Cardiac arrhythmia classification with rejection of ECG recordings based on uncertainty estimation from deep neural networks
authors: Wenrui Zhang; Xinxin Di; Guodong Wei; Shijia Geng; Zhaoji Fu; Shenda Hong
dataset_used: 2018 China Physiological Signal Challenge (CPSC) training set: 6,877 12-lead recordings (6-60 s, 500 Hz) from 11 hospitals; 9 classes (Normal, AF, AVBI, LBBB, RBBB, PAC, PVC, STD, STE); cut into 10 s segments with 4 s stride
method_or_model: 61-layer 1D CNN (7 stages of residual bottleneck blocks with grouped convolution kernel 16, SE attention, batch norm, Swish, dropout, global average pooling); Monte Carlo dropout (50 forward passes) to estimate total, data (aleatoric) and model (epistemic) uncertainty via predictive entropy; prediction with rejection when uncertainty exceeds a threshold; trained with cross-entropy then fine-tuned with ordinal loss; Adam
xai_technique: not stated as XAI (uncertainty estimation via Monte Carlo dropout; cardiologist case studies of high/low-uncertainty errors)
train_test_split: inter-patient (80% training / 10% validation / 10% test split by subjects)
key_results: Macro F1 without rejection 0.6635 (AVBI best 0.8878, STE worst 0.4103); with rejection threshold 0.400 (45.28% accepted) macro F1 0.8688 (+0.2053); F1 on accepted predictions improves 1.3-30.9% as acceptance ratio falls from 97.3% to 45.3%; FPR on accepted predictions 2.3% vs 23.3% without rejection; model and data uncertainty strongly correlated (Pearson 0.7857, p = 4.80e-245); correctly classified samples have significantly lower uncertainty (Welch's t-test p < 0.1 for all but PAC model uncertainty)
findings: Correct predictions tend to have smaller uncertainty; rejecting high-uncertainty predictions improves precision for every class; model uncertainty is lower than data uncertainty for all test samples; per cardiologist review, high data uncertainty is mainly caused by noise (large interference, baseline drift), while confident errors are mostly due to label disagreement or mixed/incomplete labels; thresholds could be set according to disease danger level
